blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Magnetic Flux

The magnetic flux linked with a surface held in a magnetic field is defined as the number of magnetic field lines crossing that surface.

Consider a plane of surface area A placed in a uniform magnetic field $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}$. If $\theta$ is the angle between the direction of the field and the area vector, Magnetic flux,  $\phi=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}}=\mathrm{BA} \cos \theta$ for N turns, the total flux linkage  $\phi= NBA \cos \theta$

Note:

Magnetic field lines are imaginary, magnetic flux is a real scalar physical quantity with dimensions

SI Unit: Weber (Wb)

CGS UNIT : Maxwell (Mx)

$\text { Conversion factor } \quad: \quad 1 \mathrm{~Wb}=10^8 \mathrm{Mx}$

If the magnetic field is non-uniform, then magnetic flux is given by  $\phi=\int \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}} \cdot \mathrm{~d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~A}}$

Gauss law in magnetism: Net magnetic flux through a closed surface is always zero.  $\phi=\oint \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{dA}}=0$

• Since incoming field lines = Outgoing field lines
    • Net flux is zero.
    • Magnetic monopoles does not exist.

$$

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: A rectangular loop of area 0.06 $m^2$ is placed in a magnetic field 1.2 T with its plane inclined 30° to the field direction. Find the flux linked with the plane of the loop.
blocks.answer:
A rectangular loop of area 0.06 $m^2$ is placed in a magnetic field 1.2 T with its plane inclined 30° to the field direction. Find the flux linked with the plane of the loop.

Area of loop: $\mathrm{A}=0.06 \mathrm{~m}^2, \mathrm{~B}=1.2 \mathrm{~T} \text { and } \theta=90^{\circ}-30^{\circ}=60^{\circ}$

So, the flux linked with the loop is

$\phi=B A \cos \theta=1.2 \times 0.06 \times \cos 60^{\circ}=1.2 \times 0.06 \times 1 / 2=0.036 \mathrm{~Wb}$

modules.name: Faraday's Law of Induction and Lenz Law

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Faraday's law:

  • Faraday's First Law of Electromagnetic Induction states that "Whenever a conductor is placed in a varying magnetic field, an electromotive force is induced.
  • Faraday's Second Law of Electromagnetic Induction states that the induced emf in a coil is equal to the rate of change of flux linkage
$|\mathrm{e}|=\dfrac{\mathrm{d} \phi}{\mathrm{dt}}$

Direction of Induced Current

Lenz Law: The polarity of induced emf is such that it tends to produce a current which opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it

$\therefore \mathrm{e}=-\dfrac{\mathrm{d} \phi}{\mathrm{dt}}$ (-ve sign is due to Lenz Law and denotes opposition)

Lenz's law follows the conservation of energy.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: Find the direction of induced current in the coil.
blocks.answer:
B is increasing so current will induce in such a way so that it opposes the magnetic field

So,

(i) induced current in the coil will be in clockwise direction.

(ii) induced current in the coil will be in Anti clockwise direction.

(ii) B is decreasing so current will induce in such a way that it opposes magnetic field B. So, the direction of the induced current is in the anti-clockwise direction.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Induced Parameters:

1. Instantaneous induced emf :

$\mathrm{e}=\operatorname{Lim}_{\Delta t \rightarrow 0}\left(\dfrac{-\Delta \phi}{\Delta t}\right)=-\dfrac{\mathrm{d} \phi}{\mathrm{dt}}$

2. Induced current flow at this instant

$I=\frac{e}{R}$

$\mathrm{I}=\frac{-1}{\mathrm{R}}\left(\frac{\mathrm{~d} \phi}{\mathrm{dt}}\right)$

3. In time interval dt, induced charge

$\mathrm{dq}=-\dfrac{\mathrm{d} \phi}{\mathrm{R}}$

4. Induced heat:-

$\mathrm{H}=\int_0^{\mathrm{t}} \mathrm{I}^2 \mathrm{Rdt}=\int_0^{\mathrm{t}} \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^2}{\mathrm{R}} \mathrm{dt}$

blocks.question: A conducting circular loop is placed in a uniform magnetic field 0.04 T with its plane perpendicular to the magnetic field. The radius of the loop starts shrinking at 2mm/s. Find the induced emf in the loop when the radius is 2 cm .

$\varepsilon=\frac{\mathrm{d} \phi}{\mathrm{dt}}=\frac{\mathrm{d}\left[(\mathrm{~B}) \pi \mathrm{r}^2\right]}{\mathrm{dt}}$

$=2 \pi \mathrm{rB}\left(\frac{\mathrm{dr}}{\mathrm{dt}}\right)$

$=(2 \pi)\left(2 \times 10^{-2}\right)\left(2 \times 10^{-3}\right)(0.04)$

$=3.2 \pi \mu \mathrm{~V}$

modules.name: Types of EMI And Self Induction

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Self Induction:

When current through the coil changes, with respect to time then magnetic flux linked with the coil also changes with respect to time. Due to this an emf and a current induced in the coil. According to Lenz law induced current opposes the change in magnetic flux. This phenomenon is called self-induction and a factor by virtue of which the coil shows opposition for change in magnetic flux called self-inductance of coil. Considering this coil circuit in two cases.

Case 1 : Current through the coil is constant

total flux of coil $(\mathrm{N} \phi) \propto$ current through the coil

$ $$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{N} \phi \propto \mathrm{I} \\ & \mathrm{~N} \phi=\mathrm{LI} \end{aligned}$$

$\mathrm{L}=\frac{\mathrm{N} \phi}{\mathrm{I}}=\frac{\mathrm{NBA}}{\mathrm{I}}=\frac{\phi_{\text {Total }}}{\mathrm{I}}$

Where {L}: self inductance of coil

Case 2 : Induced EMF in Self Induction

$\begin{aligned} & N \phi=\mathrm{LI} \\ & -\mathrm{N} \frac{\mathrm{~d} \phi}{\mathrm{dt}}=-\mathrm{L} \frac{\mathrm{~d} \mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{dt}} \text {, where }-\mathrm{N} \frac{\mathrm{~d} \phi}{\mathrm{dt}} \\ & \end{aligned}$

$ \text { called self induced emf of coil  } $$\mathrm{e}_{\mathrm{s}}=-\mathrm{L} \dfrac{\mathrm{~dI}}{\mathrm{dt}} $

Self Inductance of Circular Coil:

$\mathrm{L}=\frac{\mathrm{N} \phi}{\mathrm{I}}=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{~N}^2 \pi \mathrm{R}}{2}$

Self Inductance of Solenoid:

$\begin{aligned} & L=\frac{N \phi}{I}=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{~N}^2 A}{\ell} \\ & L=\mu_0\left(\frac{N^2}{\ell^2}\right)(\ell A)=\mu_0 n^2 A \ell=\mu_0 n^2 V \end{aligned}$

where :

A: Cross sectional area

N : number of turns

l : length of solenoid

n : turn density

Inductor:

Function of inductor is to oppose the change in current in the circuit potential difference across an inductor in the direction of current is

$V_A-V_B=L \frac{d i}{d t}$

  • If  $\dfrac{\mathrm{di}}{\mathrm{dt}}$  is +ve , potential drops from A to B.
  • If  $\dfrac{\mathrm{di}}{\mathrm{dt}}$  is -ve , potential drops from B to A.
  • If  $\dfrac{\mathrm{di}}{\mathrm{dt}}$  is zero , potential between A and B is zero.
Power in an Inductor:

$\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{LI} \frac{\mathrm{dI}}{\mathrm{dt}}+\mathrm{I}^2 \mathrm{R}$

where

$\mathrm{LI} \frac{\mathrm{dI}}{\mathrm{dt}} \rightarrow$ Power supplied to the inductor

$I^2 \mathrm{R} \rightarrow$ Power Dissipated in the resistor

Energy Stored in an Inductor:

$\mathrm{U}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{LI}^2$

Energy Density of Inductor:

Energy stored per unit volume or energy density, $\frac{U}{V}=\frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0}$

Inductor Behaviour as a Battery:

blocks.title: Important Points
blocks.text:
Its S.I. Unit is henry (H) or Wb/A.$$

• Self inductance is scalar quantity.
    • Due to self-induction, a coil opposes change in its current (due to induced emf), hence, It is also called Inertia of Electricity.
    • It is analogous to mass in mechanics.
    • L does not depend on (a) Flux ($\phi$) (b) Current (I)
    • L depends on  (a) Geometry of inductor (b) Medium$\left(\mu_0=\mu_0 \mu_r\right)$
    • Note: Self inductance is the physical property of the loop due to which it opposes the change in current that means it tries to keep the current constant. Current cannot change suddenly in the inductor.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: The current in a solenoid of 240 turns, having a length of 12 cm and a radius of 2 cm , changes at the rate of $ 0.8 \mathrm{As}^{-1}$. Find the emf induced in it.
blocks.answer:
$|\mathrm{E}|=\mathrm{L} \frac{\mathrm{dI}}{\mathrm{dt}}$

$=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{~N}^2 \mathrm{~A}}{\ell} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{dI}}{\mathrm{dt}}$

$=\frac{4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \times(240)^2 \times \pi \times(0.02)^2}{0.12} \times 0.8$

$=6 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~V}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Mutual Induction:

Whenever current passing through primary coil or circuit change with respect to time then magnetic flux in neighbouring secondary coil or circuit will also changes with respect to time. According to Lenz Law for opposition of flux change an emf and a current induced in the neighbouring coil or circuit. This phenomenon called as 'Mutual induction'.

Different mutual inductances:

  • In terms of their number of turns $\left(\mathrm{N}_1, \mathrm{~N}_2\right)$:
  • Two co-axial solenoids $\left(\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{S}_1 \mathrm{~S}_2}\right)$
Two concentric and coplanar coils $\left(M_{C_1 C_2}\right)$

  • In terms of their self-inductances $\left(\mathrm{L}_1, \mathrm{~L}_2\right)$:
Coupling Factor

• The mutual induction depends on the relative orientation of coils.
    • The coupling factor represents the fraction of flux associated with the secondary coil due to the primary coil $\mathrm{K}=\frac{\phi_{\mathrm{s}}}{\phi_{\mathrm{p}}} \leq 1$.
    • Relation between L and M, $M=K \sqrt{L_1 L_2}$

For ideal coupling $\mathrm{K}_{\max }=1 \Rightarrow \mathrm{M}_{\max }=\sqrt{\mathrm{L}_1 \mathrm{~L}_2}$ (Where M is a geometrical mean of $\mathrm{L}_1 \& \mathrm{~L}_2$)

For real coupling $(0<K<1) \Rightarrow M=K \sqrt{L_1 L_2}$

• The value of coupling factor 'K' is decided from the fashion of coupling (how flux is linked with another).

blocks.title: Important Points
blocks.text:
• Scalar Quantity.
    • SI Unit is Henry (H)
    • Mutual inductance of two coil does not depend on current through primary or flux through secondary coil.Mutual inductance is combined property of primary and secondary coil and is same for both coil.
    • For two magnetically coupled coils:

$M= \mathrm{K} \sqrt{\mathrm{~L}_1 \mathrm{~L}_2},$  where 'K' is the coupling factor.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Dynamic or Motional EMF : As this emf is produced due to the motion of a conductor, so it is called a motional emf.

The potential difference between the ends P and Q $\text { is } V=-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \cdot \vec{\ell}=(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}) \cdot \vec{\ell} \text {. }$

Important Points

$\text { If } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}} \perp \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}} \perp \vec{\ell} \text {, then } \mathrm{e}_{\text {in }}=\mathrm{vBl}_{\mathrm{eff}}$

For determining a higher potential end, evaluate $\vec{v} \times \vec{B}$

For any two points a and b, the motional emf in the direction from b to a is,

$\mathrm{e}_{\mathrm{ab}}=(\text { length of } \mathrm{ab})\left(\mathrm{v}_{\perp}\right)(\mathrm{B})$

Where $\mathrm{v}_{\perp}$= the component of velocity perpendicular to both $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}$and ab.

Motion of Straight Conductor in Horizontal Plane

For constant velocity, the resultant force on the metal rod must be zero and for that $\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{ext}}=\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{m}}$

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{m}}=\mathrm{BI} \ell \text { (Direction: opposite to motion of rod) } \\ & \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{m}}=\frac{\mathrm{B}^2 \ell^2 \mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{R}} \end{aligned}$

For the uniform motion of metal rod, the rate of doing mechanical work by an external agent or mechanical power delivered by external source is given as:

$\begin{aligned} & P_{\text {mech }}=P_{\text {ext }}=\vec{F}_{\text {ext. }} \cdot \vec{V}=F_{\text {ext }} v \\ & P_{\text {ext. }}=P_m=\frac{B^2 \ell^2 v^2}{R} \end{aligned}$

The rate of heat dissipation across resistance or thermal power developed across resistance is:

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{th}}=\mathrm{I}^2 \mathrm{R}=\mathrm{R}\left(\frac{\mathrm{Bv} \ell}{\mathrm{R}}\right)^2 \\ & \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{th}}=\frac{\mathrm{B}^2 \ell^2 \mathrm{v}^2}{\mathrm{R}} \end{aligned}$

Dynamic Induction due to Rotation of Rod

net induced e.m.f. across conducting rod $\varepsilon=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~B} \omega \ell^2$

Dynamic Induction due to Rotation of Disc

P.D. between centre and Circumference  $\mathrm{e}=\frac{\mathrm{B} \omega \mathrm{r}^2}{2}$

P.D. between two points on the circumference e= 0

Dynamic Induction due to Rotation of Cycle Wheel Spokes

$\mathrm{e}_{\mathrm{net}}=\frac{\mathrm{B} \omega \ell^2}{2}$

Special Note : - This emf does not depends on number of spokes ('N') in wheel.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Induced Electric Field

Properties of Induced Electric Field

• When magnetic field changes with time in region then an electric field induces within and outside the region.
    • $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}=\mathrm{q} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}$ is valid for this field.
    • This field is different from the conservative electrostatic field produced by stationary charges.
    • Direction of induced electric field is the same as direction of induced current.
    • Unlike electro-static field, these induced electric field lines always form closed loop and are non-conservative in nature.

Mathematical Analysis of Induced Electric field

  • $\text { For electrostatic field, } \oint \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \cdot \mathrm{~d} \vec{\ell}=0$
  • $\text { For induced electric field, } \oint \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_{\text {in }} \cdot d \vec{\ell} \neq 0$
Definition of EMF : When a charges q goes once around the loop, the total work on it by the electric field per unit charge is equal to emf in loop$$

• Inside point (r < R)

$ \mathrm{E}=\frac{\mathrm{r}}{2} \frac{\mathrm{~dB}}{\mathrm{dt}} \quad\left(\mathrm{E}_{\text {inside }} \propto \mathrm{r}\right) $

• Outside point (r > R)

$ \mathrm{E}=\frac{\mathrm{R}^2}{2 \mathrm{r}} \frac{\mathrm{~dB}}{\mathrm{dt}} \quad\left(\mathrm{E}_{\text {out }} \propto \frac{1}{\mathrm{r}}\right) $

• Surface point (r = R)

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{E}(2 \pi \mathrm{R})=\pi \mathrm{R}^2\left(\frac{\mathrm{~dB}}{\mathrm{dt}}\right) \\ & \mathrm{E}=\frac{\mathrm{R}}{2} \frac{\mathrm{~dB}}{\mathrm{dt}} \end{aligned}$

Variation of the induced electric field with r

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
When a coil, which is placed in a uniform magnetic field, rotates with constant angular frequency about the shown axis, then magnetic flux through the coil changes periodically with respect to time, so an emf of periodic nature is induced in the coil. This phenomenon is known as periodic EMI.

• Magnetic flux through the rotating coil at any instant 't' :-

$\begin{aligned} &\phi=\mathrm{NBA} \cos \theta=\mathrm{NBA} \cos \omega \mathrm{t}\\ &\text { (as } \theta=\omega t) \end{aligned}$

$\phi=\phi_0 \cos \omega \mathrm{t} \quad \text { where } \phi_0=\text { NBA is flux amplitude or max. flux }$

• Induced emf in rotating coil at any instant 't' :-

$e=-\frac{d \phi}{d t}=N B A \omega \sin \omega t$

$e=e_0 \sin \omega t \text { where } e_0=N B A \omega=\phi_0 \omega \text { is emf amplitude or max. emf }$

  • Induced current in load circuit at any instant 't' :-
$I=\frac{e}{R}=\frac{e_0}{R} \sin \omega t$

$\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{I}_0 \sin \omega t \quad \text { where } I_0=\frac{e_0}{R}=\frac{N B A \omega}{R}=\frac{\phi_0 \omega}{R} \text { is current Amplitude or max. current }$

  • Induced emf also changes in periodic manner that’s why this phenomenon called periodic EMI.
  • Phase difference between magnetic flux through the coil and induced emf is 90°.
  • $\text {  When plane of coil perpendicular to } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}} \Rightarrow \phi_{\max } \text { and } \mathrm{e}_{\min }=0$
  • $\text {  When plane of coil parallel to } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}} \Rightarrow \phi_{\min }=0 \text { and } \mathrm{e}_{\max }$
Induced emf and current acquires their max and min values simultaneously i.e. phase difference between both induced parameters is zero.

AC Generator : It converts mechanical energy into electrical energy. Its working principle is based on periodic EMI.

Losses in AC Generator

      • Iron Loss
      • Mechanical Loss

Eddy currents

Eddy currents are the currents induced in the body of a conductor when the magnetic flux linked with the conductor changes.

It is a group of induced currents which are produced, when metal bodies placed in time varying magnetic field or they moves in external magnetic field in such a way that flux through them changes with respect to time.

    • Some of the applications of eddy currents are: Electromagnetic damping, induction furnace, electromagnetic brakes, induction motor, dead beat galvanometer, speedometers and in diathermy (deep heat treatment of parts of human body).
    • Some of the undesirable effects of eddy currents are that they oppose the relative motive, involve loss of energy in the form of heat and reduce the life of electrical devices. To minimize eddy currents, laminated cores are used in a transformer.
Eddy current losses:

    • Eddy currents are induced in conductors due to changing magnetic fields.
    • These currents cause heat generation in the core of electrical machines.
    • This heat leads to energy loss and reduces machine efficiency.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
• Working principle : Mutual induction
    • Transformer has basic two section :-
    • Shell :- It consist of primary and secondary coils of copper. The effective resistance between primary and secondary coil is infinite because electric circuit between two is open

$\left(\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{ps}}=\infty\right)$

• Core :- Both Cu coils are tightly wound over a bulk metal piece of high magnetic permeability (eg. soft iron) called core. Both coils are electrically insulated to core but core part magnetically coupled to both the coils.
    • Work :-It regulates A.C. voltage and transfers the electrical power without change in frequency of input supply. (The alternating current changes itself.)
    • Special Points :-
    • It can't work with D.C. supply. If a battery is connected to its primary then output is across secondary is always zero i.e. No working of transformer.
    • It can't called 'Amplifier' as it has no power gain like transistor.
    • It has no moving part hence there are no mechanical losses in transformer, so its efficiency is higher than generator and motor.$$

• Ideal Transformer : $( \eta=100 \%)$

• No flux leakage:   $\phi_{\mathrm{s}}=\phi_{\mathrm{p}}=\dfrac{-\mathrm{d} \phi_{\mathrm{s}}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\dfrac{-\mathrm{d} \phi_{\mathrm{p}}}{\mathrm{dt}}$
    • $e_s=e_p=e \quad$ (induced emf per turn of each coil is also same)

• total induced emf for secondary $\quad \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{s}}=\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{s}} \mathrm{e}$

• total induced emf for primary $\quad \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{p}}=\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{p}} \mathrm{e}$

$\dfrac{E_n}{E_p}=\dfrac{N_p}{N_p}=n $ or p

• n : turn ratio
    • p : transformation ratio$ $

No power loss :

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{P}_{\text {out }}=\mathrm{P}_{\text {in }} \\ & \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{S}} \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{S}}=\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{P}} \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{P}} \end{aligned}$

$\dfrac{V_s}{V_p}=\dfrac{I_p}{I_s}$

$\dfrac{V_{\mathrm{s}}}{V_p}=\dfrac{I_p}{I_{\mathrm{s}}}=\dfrac{N_{\mathrm{s}}}{N_{\mathrm{p}}}=\mathrm{n} \text { or } p$

Note: Generally transformers deals in ideal condition i.e. $P_{\mathrm{in}}=P_{\text {out }}$ if other information are not given.

Real transformer$( \eta \neq 100 \% )$:- Some Some power is always lost due to flux leakage, hysteresis, eddy currents, and heating of coils. hence $\mathrm{P}_{\text {out }}<\mathrm{P}_{\text {in }} $always.

Efficiency of transformer  $\eta=\dfrac{P_{\text {out }}}{P_{\mathrm{m}}}=\dfrac{V_S I_S}{V_p I_p} \times 100$

Losses in Transformer

1. Copper or joule heating losses :-

Where : These losses occur in both coils of shell part.

Reason : Due to heating effect of current$\text { (H = I² Rt). }$

Remedy : To minimise these losses, high current coil always made up with thick wire and for removal of produced heat, circulation of mineral oil should be used.

2.Flux leakage losses :-

Where : These losses occur in between both coils of shell part.

Cause : Due to air gap between both the coils.

Remedy : To minimise these losses both coils are tightly wound over a common soft iron core (high magnetic permeability) so a closed path of magnetic field lines formed itself within the core and tries to makes coupling factor K → 1

3.Iron losses :-

Where : These losses occur in core part.

Types :

a. Hysteresis losses :-

Cause : Transformer core always present in the effect of alternating magnetic field $\left(B=B_0 \sin \omega t\right)$ so it will magnetised & demagnetised with very high frequency (f = 50 Hz). During its demagnetization a part of magnetic energy left inside core part in form of residual magnetic field. Finally, this residual energy waste as heat. Remedy : To minimise these losses material of transformer core should be such that it can be easily magnetised & demagnetised. For this purpose, magnetic soft materials should be used.

Example-Soft Iron(Low retentivity, Low coercivity

b. Eddy current losses : It is a group of induced currents which are produced, when metal bodies placed in time varying magnetic field or they moves in external magnetic field in such a way that flux through them changes with respect to time.

blocks.title: Points To Remember
blocks.text:
• These currents are produced only in closed path within the entire volume and on the surface of metal body. Therefore their measurement is impossible.
    • Circulation plane of these currents is always perpendicular to the external magnetic field direction.
    • Generally resistance of metal bodies is low so magnitude of these currents is very high.
    • These currents can heat up the metal body and some time body will melt out (Application : Induction furnace)
    • Due to these induced currents a strong eddy force (or torque) acts on metal body which always opposes the translatory (or rotatory) motion of metal body, according to Lenz law. Transformer core is always present in the effect of alternating magnetic field

$\left(B=B_0 \sin \omega t\right)$.Due to this eddy currents are produced in its volume, so a part of magnetic energy of core is wasted as heat.

Remedy : To minimise these losses transformer core should be laminated. with the help of lamination process, circulation path of eddy current is greatly reduced & net resistance of system is greatly increased. So, these currents become feeble.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Mutual Induction:

Whenever current passing through primary coil or circuit change with respect to time then magnetic flux in neighbouring secondary coil or circuit will also changes with respect to time. According to Lenz Law for opposition of flux change an emf and a current induced in the neighbouring coil or circuit. This phenomenon called as 'Mutual induction'.

Different mutual inductances:

  • In terms of their number of turns $\left(\mathrm{N}_1, \mathrm{~N}_2\right)$:
  • Two co-axial solenoids $\left(\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{S}_1 \mathrm{~S}_2}\right)$
Two concentric and coplanar coils $\left(M_{C_1 C_2}\right)$

  • In terms of their self-inductances $\left(\mathrm{L}_1, \mathrm{~L}_2\right)$:
Coupling Factor

• The mutual induction depends on the relative orientation of coils.
    • The coupling factor represents the fraction of flux associated with the secondary coil due to the primary coil $\mathrm{K}=\frac{\phi_{\mathrm{s}}}{\phi_{\mathrm{p}}} \leq 1$.
    • Relation between L and M, $M=K \sqrt{L_1 L_2}$

For ideal coupling $\mathrm{K}_{\max }=1 \Rightarrow \mathrm{M}_{\max }=\sqrt{\mathrm{L}_1 \mathrm{~L}_2}$ (Where M is a geometrical mean of $\mathrm{L}_1 \& \mathrm{~L}_2$)

For real coupling $(0<K<1) \Rightarrow M=K \sqrt{L_1 L_2}$

• The value of coupling factor 'K' is decided from the fashion of coupling (how flux is linked with another).

    • SI Unit is Henry (H)
    • Mutual inductance of two coil does not depend on current through primary or flux through secondary coil.Mutual inductance is combined property of primary and secondary coil and is same for both coil.
    • For two magnetically coupled coils:

$M= \mathrm{K} \sqrt{\mathrm{~L}_1 \mathrm{~L}_2},$  where 'K' is the coupling factor.

Magnetic Flux

The magnetic flux linked with a surface held in a magnetic field is defined as the number of magnetic field lines crossing that surface.

Consider a plane of surface area A placed in a uniform magnetic field $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}$. If $\theta$ is the angle between the direction of the field and the area vector, Magnetic flux,  $\phi=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}}=\mathrm{BA} \cos \theta$ for N turns, the total flux linkage  $\phi= NBA \cos \theta$

Note:

Magnetic field lines are imaginary, magnetic flux is a real scalar physical quantity with dimensions

SI Unit: Weber (Wb)

CGS UNIT : Maxwell (Mx)

$\text { Conversion factor } \quad: \quad 1 \mathrm{~Wb}=10^8 \mathrm{Mx}$

If the magnetic field is non-uniform, then magnetic flux is given by  $\phi=\int \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}} \cdot \mathrm{~d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~A}}$

Gauss law in magnetism: Net magnetic flux through a closed surface is always zero.  $\phi=\oint \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{dA}}=0$

• Since incoming field lines = Outgoing field lines
    • Net flux is zero.
    • Magnetic monopoles does not exist.

Faraday's law:

  • Faraday's First Law of Electromagnetic Induction states that "Whenever a conductor is placed in a varying magnetic field, an electromotive force is induced.
  • Faraday's Second Law of Electromagnetic Induction states that the induced emf in a coil is equal to the rate of change of flux linkage
$|\mathrm{e}|=\dfrac{\mathrm{d} \phi}{\mathrm{dt}}$

Direction of Induced Current

Lenz Law: The polarity of induced emf is such that it tends to produce a current which opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it

$\therefore \mathrm{e}=-\dfrac{\mathrm{d} \phi}{\mathrm{dt}}$ (-ve sign is due to Lenz Law and denotes opposition)

Lenz's law follows the conservation of energy.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Induced Parameters:

1. Instantaneous induced emf :

$\mathrm{e}=\operatorname{Lim}_{\Delta t \rightarrow 0}\left(\dfrac{-\Delta \phi}{\Delta t}\right)=-\dfrac{\mathrm{d} \phi}{\mathrm{dt}}$

2. Induced current flow at this instant

$I=\frac{e}{R}$

$\mathrm{I}=\frac{-1}{\mathrm{R}}\left(\frac{\mathrm{~d} \phi}{\mathrm{dt}}\right)$

3. In time interval dt, induced charge

$\mathrm{dq}=-\dfrac{\mathrm{d} \phi}{\mathrm{R}}$

4. Induced heat:-

$\mathrm{H}=\int_0^{\mathrm{t}} \mathrm{I}^2 \mathrm{Rdt}=\int_0^{\mathrm{t}} \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^2}{\mathrm{R}} \mathrm{dt}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Self Induction:

When current through the coil changes, with respect to time then magnetic flux linked with the coil also changes with respect to time. Due to this an emf and a current induced in the coil. According to Lenz law induced current opposes the change in magnetic flux. This phenomenon is called self-induction and a factor by virtue of which the coil shows opposition for change in magnetic flux called self-inductance of coil. Considering this coil circuit in two cases.

Case 1 : Current through the coil is constant

total flux of coil $(\mathrm{N} \phi) \propto$ current through the coil

$ $$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{N} \phi \propto \mathrm{I} \\ & \mathrm{~N} \phi=\mathrm{LI} \end{aligned}$$

$\mathrm{L}=\frac{\mathrm{N} \phi}{\mathrm{I}}=\frac{\mathrm{NBA}}{\mathrm{I}}=\frac{\phi_{\text {Total }}}{\mathrm{I}}$

Where {L}: self inductance of coil

Case 2 : Induced EMF in Self Induction

$\begin{aligned} & N \phi=\mathrm{LI} \\ & -\mathrm{N} \frac{\mathrm{~d} \phi}{\mathrm{dt}}=-\mathrm{L} \frac{\mathrm{~d} \mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{dt}} \text {, where }-\mathrm{N} \frac{\mathrm{~d} \phi}{\mathrm{dt}} \\ & \end{aligned}$

$ \text { called self induced emf of coil  } $$\mathrm{e}_{\mathrm{s}}=-\mathrm{L} \dfrac{\mathrm{~dI}}{\mathrm{dt}} $

Self Inductance of Circular Coil:

$\mathrm{L}=\frac{\mathrm{N} \phi}{\mathrm{I}}=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{~N}^2 \pi \mathrm{R}}{2}$

Self Inductance of Solenoid:

$\begin{aligned} & L=\frac{N \phi}{I}=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{~N}^2 A}{\ell} \\ & L=\mu_0\left(\frac{N^2}{\ell^2}\right)(\ell A)=\mu_0 n^2 A \ell=\mu_0 n^2 V \end{aligned}$

where :

A: Cross sectional area

N : number of turns

l : length of solenoid

n : turn density

Inductor:

Function of inductor is to oppose the change in current in the circuit potential difference across an inductor in the direction of current is

$V_A-V_B=L \frac{d i}{d t}$

  • If  $\dfrac{\mathrm{di}}{\mathrm{dt}}$  is +ve , potential drops from A to B.
  • If  $\dfrac{\mathrm{di}}{\mathrm{dt}}$  is -ve , potential drops from B to A.
  • If  $\dfrac{\mathrm{di}}{\mathrm{dt}}$  is zero , potential between A and B is zero.
Power in an Inductor:

$\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{LI} \frac{\mathrm{dI}}{\mathrm{dt}}+\mathrm{I}^2 \mathrm{R}$

where

$\mathrm{LI} \frac{\mathrm{dI}}{\mathrm{dt}} \rightarrow$ Power supplied to the inductor

$I^2 \mathrm{R} \rightarrow$ Power Dissipated in the resistor

Energy Stored in an Inductor:

$\mathrm{U}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{LI}^2$

Energy Density of Inductor:

Energy stored per unit volume or energy density, $\frac{U}{V}=\frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Dynamic or Motional EMF : As this emf is produced due to the motion of a conductor, so it is called a motional emf.

The potential difference between the ends P and Q $\text { is } V=-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \cdot \vec{\ell}=(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}) \cdot \vec{\ell} \text {. }$

Important Points

$\text { If } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}} \perp \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}} \perp \vec{\ell} \text {, then } \mathrm{e}_{\text {in }}=\mathrm{vBl}_{\mathrm{eff}}$

For determining a higher potential end, evaluate $\vec{v} \times \vec{B}$

For any two points a and b, the motional emf in the direction from b to a is,

$\mathrm{e}_{\mathrm{ab}}=(\text { length of } \mathrm{ab})\left(\mathrm{v}_{\perp}\right)(\mathrm{B})$

Where $\mathrm{v}_{\perp}$= the component of velocity perpendicular to both $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}$and ab.

Motion of Straight Conductor in Horizontal Plane

For constant velocity, the resultant force on the metal rod must be zero and for that $\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{ext}}=\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{m}}$

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{m}}=\mathrm{BI} \ell \text { (Direction: opposite to motion of rod) } \\ & \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{m}}=\frac{\mathrm{B}^2 \ell^2 \mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{R}} \end{aligned}$

For the uniform motion of metal rod, the rate of doing mechanical work by an external agent or mechanical power delivered by external source is given as:

$\begin{aligned} & P_{\text {mech }}=P_{\text {ext }}=\vec{F}_{\text {ext. }} \cdot \vec{V}=F_{\text {ext }} v \\ & P_{\text {ext. }}=P_m=\frac{B^2 \ell^2 v^2}{R} \end{aligned}$

The rate of heat dissipation across resistance or thermal power developed across resistance is:

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{th}}=\mathrm{I}^2 \mathrm{R}=\mathrm{R}\left(\frac{\mathrm{Bv} \ell}{\mathrm{R}}\right)^2 \\ & \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{th}}=\frac{\mathrm{B}^2 \ell^2 \mathrm{v}^2}{\mathrm{R}} \end{aligned}$

Dynamic Induction due to Rotation of Rod

net induced e.m.f. across conducting rod $\varepsilon=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~B} \omega \ell^2$

Dynamic Induction due to Rotation of Disc

P.D. between centre and Circumference  $\mathrm{e}=\frac{\mathrm{B} \omega \mathrm{r}^2}{2}$

P.D. between two points on the circumference e= 0

Dynamic Induction due to Rotation of Cycle Wheel Spokes

$\mathrm{e}_{\mathrm{net}}=\frac{\mathrm{B} \omega \ell^2}{2}$

Special Note : - This emf does not depends on number of spokes ('N') in wheel.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Induced Electric Field

Properties of Induced Electric Field

• When magnetic field changes with time in region then an electric field induces within and outside the region.
    • $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}=\mathrm{q} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}$ is valid for this field.
    • This field is different from the conservative electrostatic field produced by stationary charges.
    • Direction of induced electric field is the same as direction of induced current.
    • Unlike electro-static field, these induced electric field lines always form closed loop and are non-conservative in nature.

Mathematical Analysis of Induced Electric field

  • $\text { For electrostatic field, } \oint \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \cdot \mathrm{~d} \vec{\ell}=0$
  • $\text { For induced electric field, } \oint \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_{\text {in }} \cdot d \vec{\ell} \neq 0$
Definition of EMF : When a charges q goes once around the loop, the total work on it by the electric field per unit charge is equal to emf in loop$$

• Inside point (r < R)

$ \mathrm{E}=\frac{\mathrm{r}}{2} \frac{\mathrm{~dB}}{\mathrm{dt}} \quad\left(\mathrm{E}_{\text {inside }} \propto \mathrm{r}\right) $

• Outside point (r > R)

$ \mathrm{E}=\frac{\mathrm{R}^2}{2 \mathrm{r}} \frac{\mathrm{~dB}}{\mathrm{dt}} \quad\left(\mathrm{E}_{\text {out }} \propto \frac{1}{\mathrm{r}}\right) $

• Surface point (r = R)

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{E}(2 \pi \mathrm{R})=\pi \mathrm{R}^2\left(\frac{\mathrm{~dB}}{\mathrm{dt}}\right) \\ & \mathrm{E}=\frac{\mathrm{R}}{2} \frac{\mathrm{~dB}}{\mathrm{dt}} \end{aligned}$

    • It can't called 'Amplifier' as it has no power gain like transistor.
    • It has no moving part hence there are no mechanical losses in transformer, so its efficiency is higher than generator and motor.$$

• Ideal Transformer : $( \eta=100 \%)$

• No flux leakage:   $\phi_{\mathrm{s}}=\phi_{\mathrm{p}}=\dfrac{-\mathrm{d} \phi_{\mathrm{s}}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\dfrac{-\mathrm{d} \phi_{\mathrm{p}}}{\mathrm{dt}}$
    • $e_s=e_p=e \quad$ (induced emf per turn of each coil is also same)

• total induced emf for secondary $\quad \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{s}}=\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{s}} \mathrm{e}$

• total induced emf for primary $\quad \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{p}}=\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{p}} \mathrm{e}$

$\dfrac{E_n}{E_p}=\dfrac{N_p}{N_p}=n $ or p

• n : turn ratio
    • p : transformation ratio$ $

No power loss :

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{P}_{\text {out }}=\mathrm{P}_{\text {in }} \\ & \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{S}} \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{S}}=\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{P}} \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{P}} \end{aligned}$

$\dfrac{V_s}{V_p}=\dfrac{I_p}{I_s}$

$\dfrac{V_{\mathrm{s}}}{V_p}=\dfrac{I_p}{I_{\mathrm{s}}}=\dfrac{N_{\mathrm{s}}}{N_{\mathrm{p}}}=\mathrm{n} \text { or } p$

Note: Generally transformers deals in ideal condition i.e. $P_{\mathrm{in}}=P_{\text {out }}$ if other information are not given.

Real transformer$( \eta \neq 100 \% )$:- Some Some power is always lost due to flux leakage, hysteresis, eddy currents, and heating of coils. hence $\mathrm{P}_{\text {out }}<\mathrm{P}_{\text {in }} $always.

Efficiency of transformer  $\eta=\dfrac{P_{\text {out }}}{P_{\mathrm{m}}}=\dfrac{V_S I_S}{V_p I_p} \times 100$

Losses in Transformer

1. Copper or joule heating losses :-

Where : These losses occur in both coils of shell part.

Reason : Due to heating effect of current$\text { (H = I² Rt). }$

Remedy : To minimise these losses, high current coil always made up with thick wire and for removal of produced heat, circulation of mineral oil should be used.

2.Flux leakage losses :-

Where : These losses occur in between both coils of shell part.

Cause : Due to air gap between both the coils.

Remedy : To minimise these losses both coils are tightly wound over a common soft iron core (high magnetic permeability) so a closed path of magnetic field lines formed itself within the core and tries to makes coupling factor K → 1

3.Iron losses :-

Where : These losses occur in core part.

Types :

a. Hysteresis losses :-

Cause : Transformer core always present in the effect of alternating magnetic field $\left(B=B_0 \sin \omega t\right)$ so it will magnetised & demagnetised with very high frequency (f = 50 Hz). During its demagnetization a part of magnetic energy left inside core part in form of residual magnetic field. Finally, this residual energy waste as heat. Remedy : To minimise these losses material of transformer core should be such that it can be easily magnetised & demagnetised. For this purpose, magnetic soft materials should be used.

Example-Soft Iron(Low retentivity, Low coercivity

b. Eddy current losses : It is a group of induced currents which are produced, when metal bodies placed in time varying magnetic field or they moves in external magnetic field in such a way that flux through them changes with respect to time.
